title: Stratigraphy & Age Dating
intro: How do we know the order of Earth's events and how many years ago they happened? Learn the rules for older vs younger (relative dating), the gaps in the record (unconformities), and how radioactive clocks give real ages (half-life, isotopes, closure temperature).

sections.title: Deep time: why geology needs a huge clock

boxes.text: Why does this matter? Rocks record events one on top of another, but a rock does not come with a date stamp. To tell the story of Earth you need two tools: an ORDER of events (relative dating) and a NUMBER of years (numerical dating). This whole chapter is those two tools.
Think of the rock record as a very long story. Relative dating tells you the order of the chapters. Numerical dating tells you the date written on some pages.

images.alt: Tall block diagram of Earth's history showing the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic with ages in millions of years.
A short list of extra topics that are not covered in this chapter.

steps.title: The geologic column
bullets: The **geologic column** is a tall stack of time blocks: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic. The first three together are the Precambrian.
Units: ka = thousand years ago, **Ma** = million years ago, **Ga** = billion years ago.
The bottom of the column is the birth of the Earth, about 4,570 Ma.

img.alt: A short list of extra topics that are not covered in this chapter.

steps.title: Topics this chapter leaves out
bullets: Not covered here: the evolution of planets, stars, solar systems, galaxies and the universe, and how Earth interacts with the solar system.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Deep time** = the immense span of geologic time. Human history is a tiny blip next to it. Our feeling for time is weeks, years, decades and a few generations, but deep time is **billions of years**.
Geologic time gives a frame of reference for **rocks, fossils, geologic structures, landscapes, tectonic events and processes of change**.

boxes.text: Why can we read old rocks at all? Because nature did not change the rules. If mud cracks when it dries now, then cracked mud in a very old rock also dried in the sun. We use today's rain, rivers and volcanoes to explain old rocks.

Do not mix up the names. Hutton = uniformitarianism ('Father of Modern Geology'). Lyell = wrote the textbook that set the relative-dating principles. William 'Strata' Smith (slide 51) = first geologic map.
Relative = 'older than / younger than', like saying you are older than your cousin. Numerical = 'I am 22 years old'.

Photos of mudcracks drying today next to mudcracks preserved in ancient rock.
Cliff cross-section with layers, a basalt dike, fossil bones and labelled ages of granite, dike and volcanic ash.

steps.title: The present is the key to the past
bullets: 'The present is the key to the past' is the short version of uniformitarianism: the processes we see today are the same as those that worked long ago.
Geologic change is slow, so big changes need a long time.
Hutton wrote: 'We find no vestige of a beginning; no prospect of an end.'

img.alt: Photos of mudcracks drying today next to mudcracks preserved in ancient rock.

steps.title: Uniformitarianism and Lyell
bullets: The **Principle of Uniformitarianism** says processes observed today were the same in the past. Example: mudcracks in ancient sediments formed just like mudcracks drying today.
**Sir Charles Lyell** wrote Principles of Geology (1830-33). He set out physical principles for working out relative ages, and they are still used.

img.alt: Cliff cross-section with layers, a basalt dike, fossil bones and labelled ages of granite, dike and volcanic ash.

steps.title: Relative vs numerical dating
bullets: **Relative dating** = qualitative (older or younger), developed hundreds of years ago. **Numerical dating** = quantitative (a number of years), developed in the last 70 years. Geologists use both.
In this cliff, the layers are ordered by position, and some rocks also have real ages: granite 125 Ma, basalt dike 80 Ma, volcanic ash 50 Ma.
Fossil bones are the same age as the Cretaceous sandstone they lie in.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **James Hutton** (1726-97), a Scottish physician and farmer, first stated uniformitarianism. He saw that vast time was needed to make rocks, so he is the 'Father of Modern Geology'.

sections.title: The principles of relative dating

boxes.text: Why does superposition work? Pour coloured sand into a jar: the first sand is on the bottom, the last on top. Each new layer can only land on something that already exists.
Why does cross-cutting work? You cannot cut a cake that has not been baked. A dike needs rock to push into, so the rock was there first.
Inclusions: the chocolate chips are older than the cookie dough. Baked contact: the toast is older than the heat that toasted it.

Superposition only works in an UNDEFORMED sequence. If beds were folded upside down, youngest is not on top (that is why 'younging' features matter). Also watch exam wording: 'xenoliths are YOUNGER than the intrusion' is wrong, they are OLDER.

sourceNotes: Textbook lists five principles (superposition, original horizontality, lateral continuity, cross-cutting, inclusions) plus fossil succession. The slides add baked contacts as its own principle.

steps.title: Flat layers, youngest on top
bullets: **Original horizontality**: sediments settle out of a fluid by gravity, so they pile up flat. Sediment does not favour a slope, so most sedimentary beds started horizontal.
**Superposition**: in an undeformed sequence, each bed is older than the one above and younger than the one below. Youngest on top, oldest at the bottom.

img.alt: Close-up of tilted red sandstone beds with fine internal layering.

steps.title: 'Younging' features
bullets: **'Younging' features** show which way is younger, even if the rocks are tilted upside down.

img.alt: Diagram of a wide layered sheet later cut by a valley, above a Grand Canyon photo with the Kaibab, Coconino and Hermit layers labelled.

steps.title: Lateral continuity
bullets: **Lateral continuity**: strata form wide horizontal sheets.
Later erosion cuts them up (a canyon, for example), but the same layer on both sides was once joined.
Grand Canyon: the Kaibab, Coconino and Hermit layers match across the canyon.

steps.title: Cross-cutting relations
bullets: **Cross-cutting relations**: younger features cut across older ones. A fault, dike or erosion surface is younger than what it cuts.
'A dyke cannot intrude rocks that aren't there yet.'

steps.title: Baked contacts and inclusions
bullets: **Baked contacts**: an igneous intrusion cooks the country rock it enters, so the baked rock is older. A **chill margin** forms inside the intrusion edge from rapid cooling.
**Inclusions**: a fragment inside another rock is older than the rock around it. Weathered rubble came from older rock.
**Xenoliths** inside an intrusion are older than the intrusion.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The principles covered here are original horizontality, superposition, lateral continuity, cross-cutting relations, baked contacts and inclusions. Fossil succession (next topic) is one more.

boxes.text: Why do unconformities matter? Each wavy line means 'rocks that should be here are missing'. The time is still there, but no rock recorded it. Angular unconformity story: deposit flat, squeeze and tilt, erode flat, deposit again.

Look at what is BELOW the line. Tilted sedimentary layers = ANGULAR. Granite or gneiss (crystalline) = NON-conformity ('non-sedimentary' below). Parallel sedimentary layers = DIS-conformity (looks almost normal).

The textbook says the Grand Canyon 'Great Unconformity' is an angular unconformity (tilted strata below flat strata) and the Grand Canyon Supergroup on Vishnu schist is a nonconformity. Do not call every wavy line an angular unconformity: check what is below it.

images.alt: Photo and sketch of vertical sandstone layers overlain by gently tilted red layers at Siccar Point, Scotland.
Photo of sandstone resting on granite beside a three-step diagram of a nonconformity forming.
Diagrams of sea level dropping and rising above a red rock face with a channel surface and a paleosol horizon labelled.

img.alt: Photo and sketch of vertical sandstone layers overlain by gently tilted red layers at Siccar Point, Scotland.

steps.title: Angular unconformity
bullets: **Angular unconformity**: old strata are folded or tilted, mountains are eroded flat, then new horizontal beds are laid on top. Layers below are at an ANGLE to layers above.
It is a 'huge gulf in geologic time'. Hutton first saw its meaning.
**Hutton's Unconformity**, Siccar Point, Scotland: vertical Ordovician sandstone is overlain by gently dipping Devonian redbeds. Missing time = **50 million years**.

img.alt: Photo of sandstone resting on granite beside a three-step diagram of a nonconformity forming.

steps.title: Nonconformity
bullets: **Nonconformity**: sedimentary rock sits on **igneous or metamorphic** rock (for example sandstone on granite).
Erosion exposed the crystalline rock first. Then the sea returned and sediment was deposited on the eroded surface.

img.alt: Diagrams of sea level dropping and rising above a red rock face with a channel surface and a paleosol horizon labelled.

steps.title: Disconformity
bullets: **Disconformity**: a gap between PARALLEL sedimentary layers because sedimentation stopped or erosion removed some. Often subtle.
Clues: an eroded channel surface and an old soil (paleosol horizon).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: An **unconformity** = a time gap in the rock record, from nondeposition or erosion. Three types: angular unconformity, nonconformity and disconformity.

sections.title: Putting the principles together

boxes.text: Method: start at the bottom, then ask of every feature 'what does it cut, bake, contain or lie on?' The thing doing the cutting or baking or containing is the younger one. Build the story from oldest to youngest.
A fault is younger than everything it cuts. A dike that cuts the fault with no offset is younger than the fault. Always check which one is displaced.

sourceNotes: Worked example from Intro to Geology 7.1.3 (gneiss, fault A, batholith B ...).

images.alt: Block diagram showing folded layers, a granite pluton, a sill, a basalt dike and a fault.
Three cross-sections: layers pile up, a sill intrudes, then the whole stack is folded.
Cross-sections showing a granite pluton intruding, a fault cutting it, then a basalt dike feeding a volcano.

img.alt: Block diagram showing folded layers, a granite pluton, a sill, a basalt dike and a fault.

steps.title: Reading a block diagram
bullets: This block shows folded sediments, intrusions, granite, basalt, a fault, xenoliths, inclusions and a baked contact.
The physical principles let us sort out the relative ages with ease, even in a complex block.

img.alt: Three cross-sections: layers pile up, a sill intrudes, then the whole stack is folded.

steps.title: Events 1 to 3
bullets: (1) Horizontal strata pile up. Number 1 is oldest (superposition).
(2) An igneous **sill** intrudes. Pieces of beds 4 and 5 inside the sill (inclusions) prove the sill is younger.
(3) Folding, uplift and erosion happen. The sill is itself folded, so folding came after the sill.

img.alt: Cross-sections showing a granite pluton intruding, a fault cutting it, then a basalt dike feeding a volcano.

steps.title: Events 4 to 6
bullets: (4) A **granitic pluton** intrudes the folded sediments. Xenoliths fall into the magma and it bakes the country rock.
(5) A **fault** cuts the pluton and the folded sediments.
(6) A **basalt dike** cuts across the block and feeds a volcano. Then the dike cools and the volcano and land erode.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: A similar worked example reads oldest to youngest: gneiss, fault A, batholith B, erosion (nonconformity), sediment C, dike D, a disconformity, sediment E, fault F, and modern erosion.

boxes.text: Why do fossils date rocks? Evolution does not repeat. A species that lived 10 million years is only in rocks of that age. Find it in two far apart places and those beds are the same age.
Index fossil = a 'time stamp' fossil. Wide place (found everywhere), short time (narrow age): easy to match.
A fossil that lived a very long time is a poor index fossil, even if common. Short range and wide distribution make a good one. Fossils give RELATIVE ages unless tied to dated rocks.

images.alt: Collage of fossils: an ammonite, a shell, a dinosaur skeleton and a dinosaur footprint.
A mounted dinosaur skeleton in a museum, with text about fossil succession.
Text naming the first appearance datum (FAD) and the last appearance datum (LAD).

img.alt: Collage of fossils: an ammonite, a shell, a dinosaur skeleton and a dinosaur footprint.

bullets: **Principle of Fossil Succession**: fossils appear in a predictable order through time.
Specific fossils are found only in a limited, often narrow, time range, so they are time markers.
**Index fossils** are diagnostic of a particular geologic time. The best ones are widespread AND lived only a short time (for example foraminifera and conodonts).

img.alt: A mounted dinosaur skeleton in a museum, with text about fossil succession.

steps.title: Species come and go
bullets: Species **evolve, exist for a time, then disappear forever**. Time periods are recognised by their fossil content.
**Fossil range** = first to last appearance of a species. Each fossil has its own range, and ranges of different species may overlap.
Where two ranges overlap, you can pin the bed to the overlap.

img.alt: Text naming the first appearance datum (FAD) and the last appearance datum (LAD).

steps.title: FAD and LAD
bullets: **FAD** = first appearance datum. **LAD** = last appearance datum.
They mark where a species first and last appears in the rock record.

sections.title: Stratigraphic correlation and geologic maps

boxes.text: Why can rock types differ but be the same age? Beach, reef and deep sea all exist on the same day. Sand forms at the beach, limestone at the reef, mud in deep water. One time line cuts across three rock types.
Lithologic correlation matches ROCK TYPE. Chronostratigraphic matches AGE. They are not always the same: same-age rocks can look different in different places.
'Strata' Smith = first map of strata, 1815.

sourceNotes: Textbook 7.4.3: correlation types, transgression and regression. The slides do not cover Walther's law by name.

images.alt: Grand Canyon photo with a labelled sketch of its rock formations, from the Kaibab at the top to the Vishnu Schist at the bottom.
A Grand Canyon rock column on the left linked by grey bands to a time scale on the right, with gaps marked 'No rock preserved'.
Labelled stratigraphic column of the Grand Canyon with formations, groups and rock types.

steps.title: Formations in the Grand Canyon
bullets: A **formation** is a rock unit recognised by notable changes in rock type and fossils.
The Grand Canyon is divided into formations such as Kaibab, Toroweap, Coconino, Hermit, Supai, Redwall, Muav, Bright Angel and Tapeats.

img.alt: A Grand Canyon rock column on the left linked by grey bands to a time scale on the right, with gaps marked 'No rock preserved'.

steps.title: Gaps in the record
bullets: Grey bands link each Grand Canyon formation (left) to its place in time (right).
Big gaps marked 'No rock preserved' are missing time.
Sea level rising (**transgression**) lays down marine strata. Sea level falling (**regression**) exposes land to erosion and makes unconformities.

img.alt: Labelled stratigraphic column of the Grand Canyon with formations, groups and rock types.

steps.title: Stratigraphic columns
bullets: A **stratigraphic column** shows the sequence of strata.
Formations can be traced over long distances. Several formations may be combined as a **group** (for example the Supai Group).

steps.title: Matching by rock type
bullets: **Lithologic correlation**: match units by rock type. Columns kilometres apart look slightly different, but units can still be matched.
Some units thicken, thin or **pinch out**. Thinning toward column C suggests a basin tapered that way.
Columns from Arizona and Utah national parks (Grand Canyon, Zion, Bryce, Cedar Breaks) overlap and build a **composite** column.
**William 'Strata' Smith** matched rocks by type and distinctive fossils in Great Britain. He compiled the first geologic map in **1815**.
Maps use colour for rock units. A block diagram shows the cross section under the map surface.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Correlation** = deciding that strata in different places are the same age.
Kinds of correlation: **lithostratigraphic** (same rock type), **chronostratigraphic** (same age, maybe different rock) and biostratigraphic (matched with index fossils).

sections.title: The geologic column and time scale

boxes.text: Why does the time scale have a fossil basis? Eras and periods were named from fossil content, in a known order, before any numbers existed. Numbers were added later.

Slide 68 prints the Hadean/Archean boundary near 4.1 Ga, while the Earth Biography lecture uses 3.8 Ga. Slide 68 also shows 542 Ma while the textbook says about 541 Ma. Use the slide's numbers for this chapter.
Big to small: Eon, Era, Period, Epoch. Each one is a subdivision of the one before it.

images.alt: Chart of the geologic column with eons, eras, periods and epochs, and a world map of rock columns being stacked together.
Spiral drawing of life through geologic time, from single cells and the Cambrian explosion to dinosaurs and mammals.
Detailed chart of the geologic time scale with eons, eras, periods and epochs and their boundary ages in millions of years.

img.alt: Chart of the geologic column with eons, eras, periods and epochs, and a world map of rock columns being stacked together.

bullets: The **geologic column** is a composite built from incomplete sections around the world. Correlation stacks them into one sequence covering almost all of Earth history.
The **geologic time scale** divides the column into blocks, like Earth's calendar. Biggest to smallest: Eon, Era, Period, Epoch.
Typical sizes: eon hundreds to thousands of Ma, era 65 to hundreds of Ma, period 2 to 70 Ma, epoch 0.011 to 22 Ma.

img.alt: Spiral drawing of life through geologic time, from single cells and the Cambrian explosion to dinosaurs and mammals.

steps.title: Life through time
bullets: Life first appeared about **3.8 Ga** as single cells.
O2 from bacteria built up in the atmosphere by **2 Ga**. Multicellular life evolved around 700 Ma.
About **542 Ma** hard shells appear. Shells improve preservation, and life diversifies fast: the **Cambrian explosion**.

img.alt: Detailed chart of the geologic time scale with eons, eras, periods and epochs and their boundary ages in millions of years.

bullets: Phanerozoic = Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic. Boundary ages: **542 Ma** (start of Phanerozoic and Cambrian), **251.0 Ma** (Paleozoic to Mesozoic), 65.5 Ma (Mesozoic to Cenozoic).
The Jurassic starts at 199.6 Ma and the Cretaceous at 145.5 Ma.
The Proterozoic to Archean boundary is 2,500 Ma, and the Earth begins about 4,600 Ma.

boxes.text: Why is it a clock? Think of popcorn popping: you cannot say when one kernel pops, but with thousands you know about half pop in a set time. A crystal that starts with only parent atoms (no daughter) starts the clock. More daughter means more time.
Halving staircase: 100% then 50% then 25% then 12.5% then 6.25%. Parent halves each half-life, daughter fills the gap (daughter = 100 minus parent).
Half-life is NOT half the age. After two half-lives the parent is 1/4, not zero. Also the half-life is a fixed property of the isotope: it does not change with how much you have.

images.alt: A hand holding several rock samples with yellow-green stains.
A person holding a radiation counter and probe against a rock.
Scientists working in an isotope laboratory with a table of isotopes and half-lives.

img.alt: A hand holding several rock samples with yellow-green stains.

steps.title: Radiometric dating
bullets: Many relative ages can be given real dates by **radiometric dating** (also called **geochronology**).
It measures radioactive isotopes in minerals. They decay at a known fixed rate, so they act as **internal clocks**.

img.alt: A person holding a radiation counter and probe against a rock.

steps.title: Isotopes
bullets: **Isotopes** = atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.
**Stable** isotopes (13C) never change. **Radioactive** isotopes (14C) spontaneously decay into other elements.
Decay goes along a decay chain to a stable end point. The **parent** isotope is the one that decays. The **daughter** isotope is the product.
**Half-life** = time for half of the unstable nuclei to decay. It is unique to each isotope. As the parent shrinks, the daughter 'grows in'.
The decay of a single atom is random, but a huge number of atoms decays predictably.

steps.title: Counting half-lives
bullets: After **1 half-life** 1/2 of the parent remains, after 2 it is 1/4, and after 3 it is **1/8**.
As a parent : daughter graph this goes 16:0, 8:8, 4:12, 2:14, 1:15.
After about 10 half-lives too little parent remains to measure.

img.alt: Scientists working in an isotope laboratory with a table of isotopes and half-lives.

steps.title: Age from the ratio
bullets: The age of a mineral comes from the **ratio of parent to daughter** isotopes plus the known half-life of the parent.
This work needs very precise lab measurements.

sections.title: Isotope systems, closure temperature and other methods

boxes.text: Why closure temperature? In a hot crystal atoms leak in and out, so the clock cannot start. When it cools below the closure temperature, the atoms are locked and the clock starts. An igneous date = when the magma cooled.

Why do we date ash and dikes, not sandstone? Sandstone grains came from older rocks, so their dates give the age of the SOURCE. A volcanic ash or lava flow in the sequence, or a dike cutting it, has a clean crystallisation age. Lava below and ash above the sandstone brackets it between those ages.

Slide vs textbook values differ: 40K half-life 1.3 billion (slide) vs 1.25 billion (textbook). 235U 713 million (slide) vs 704 million (textbook). Use the slide numbers. 14C (5,730 years) is only in the textbook.

Pick the clock to match the age: C-14 for recent bones and wood (tens of thousands of years), U-Pb or K-Ar for millions to billions of years. A half-life far too long or too short for your sample gives no useful answer.

sourceNotes: 14C row and 14C details are textbook only (not in the slide's Table 10.1; the slide only names 14C as radioactive). Textbook values: 40K 1.25 billion, 235U 704 million.

steps.title: Isotopic date and closure temperature
bullets: An **isotopic date** is the time a mineral began to keep ALL its parent and daughter atoms.
That needs cooling below a **closure temperature**. If the rock is reheated, the clock can be reset.
Best rocks for dating: igneous and metamorphic. Sedimentary rocks can only rarely be dated directly.

img.alt: Diagrams of living, dead and buried trees with matching ring patterns, plus a clam shell, a tree cross-section and layered glacier ice.

steps.title: Counting rings and layers
bullets: Numerical ages are possible without isotopes, but they have a **very limited range**.
Count annual growth rings of trees or shells to establish dates.
Rhythmic layers can be counted too, such as annual layers in ice.

img.alt: Banded sedimentary rock face with thin repeating layers.

steps.title: Varves
bullets: **Varves** are annual layers in sediment. Counting them gives a numerical age.

steps.title: Bracketing sediments
bullets: Sediments are **bracketed** by dating materials that cross-cut them or lie in them, such as volcanic ash (50 Ma), basalt dike (80 Ma) and granite (125 Ma).
Age ranges narrow as more data accumulates.
**Carbon-14** has a half-life of **5,730 years**. It is used for organic things (wood, bone) up to about 57,300 years (10 half-lives).
14C forms in the air when cosmic rays hit 14N. Living things keep the 14C/12C ratio until death, then the clock starts.
**Luminescence** dates buried sediment younger than 1 million years. **Fission track** dates apatite and others, about 100,000 to 2 billion years.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Half-lives of the main isotope systems: 147Sm to 143Nd = 106 billion years (garnets, micas). 87Rb to 87Sr = 48.8 billion (K-bearing minerals: mica, feldspar, hornblende). **238U to 206Pb = 4.5 billion** (zircon, uraninite). 40K to 40Ar = 1.3 billion (mica, feldspar, hornblende). **235U to 207Pb = 713 million** (zircon, uraninite).
Zircon is useful for dating because it is tough and holds uranium.

sections.title: Age of the Earth and review questions

boxes.text: Why meteorites and moon rocks? Earth's own rocks are recycled by plate tectonics, so the oldest we find are younger than the planet. Meteorites are leftovers from when the solar system formed, so they keep the original age.

Three different old numbers: 4.03 Ga oldest ROCKS, 4.4 Ga oldest ZIRCON grains, 4.57 Ga age of the EARTH (slide). The textbook says 4.54 billion for Earth and calls the 4.4 Ga zircons the oldest known 'rocks'. Use the slide: Earth 4.57 Ga.
The numbers climb: 4.03 rocks, 4.4 zircon, 4.57 Earth.

sourceNotes: Textbook 7.2.3: Patterson 4.55 billion (give or take 70 million); current estimate 4.54 billion plus or minus 50 million.

images.alt: A multiple-choice question asking the age of the Earth.
A multiple-choice question about what relative ages let us find out.

img.alt: A multiple-choice question asking the age of the Earth.

steps.title: How old is the Earth?
bullets: The **oldest rocks on Earth's surface** are 4.03 Ga. **Zircons** in ancient sandstones are 4.4 Ga.
The **age of Earth = 4.57 Ga**, from correlation with meteorites and moon rocks. In round numbers, about 4.5 billion years.
Clair Patterson used U-Pb dating on meteorites and got about 4.55 billion years.

img.alt: A multiple-choice question about what relative ages let us find out.

steps.title: What relative ages tell us
bullets: Relative ages let us find out which of two side-by-side rocks is younger and which is older.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: About 80% of today's continental area was in place by the end of the Archean. Archean provinces on the map of North America are older than 2.5 Ga.
Lateral continuity review: a layer cut by a valley can be assumed to have once spanned the gap.

Measures radioactive isotopes in minerals that decay at a known fixed rate. They act as internal clocks.
Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers. Stable (13C) or radioactive (14C).
Parent = the isotope that decays. Daughter = the decay product. A decay chain ends at a stable isotope.
Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay. Unique to each isotope. After 3 half-lives, 1/8 of the parent remains.
cards.short: Time for half the parent to decay

cards.back: Measure the parent to daughter ratio and use the parent's known half-life.
cards.short: Parent to daughter ratio gives age

cards.back: The mineral must cool below it to keep all parent and daughter atoms. Reheating can reset the clock.
Igneous and metamorphic rocks. Sedimentary rocks can only rarely be dated directly.
147Sm 106 billion y; 87Rb 48.8 billion; 238U 4.5 billion; 40K 1.3 billion; 235U 713 million.
Half-life 5,730 years, for organic material (wood, bone) up to about 57,300 years. 14C decays to 14N.
Count tree rings, shell growth rings, or annual layers (varves, ice layers). Very limited range.
Date igneous materials that cut or lie in the sediments, such as ash, dikes and lava. The age range narrows with more data.
cards.short: Date ash or dikes around sediment

cards.back: 4.57 Ga, from correlation with meteorites and moon rocks. Oldest rocks 4.03 Ga, zircons 4.4 Ga.

quiz.q: Which principle states that younger features cut across older ones?
quiz.why: A dike, fault or erosion surface cannot cut rock that is not there yet, so it must be younger than what it cuts.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a principle of relative dating?
options: The half-life of a parent isotope
quiz.why: Half-life belongs to numerical (radiometric) dating. The others are relative-dating principles.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements:
I. Xenoliths in an intrusion are older than the intrusion.
II. A dike is younger than the rock it cuts.
III. Baked country rock is younger than the intrusion that baked it.
quiz.why: I (inclusions) and II (cross-cutting) are correct. III is wrong: the baked rock had to exist before it could be baked.

quiz.q: Horizontal sandstone lies directly on eroded granite. What type of contact is this?
quiz.why: Sedimentary rock on crystalline igneous (or metamorphic) rock is a nonconformity.

quiz.q: Which statement about unconformities is INCORRECT?
options: A disconformity always has tilted layers below the gap.
An unconformity is a time gap from nondeposition or erosion.
An angular unconformity has tilted strata below flat strata.
A nonconformity has sedimentary rock above igneous or metamorphic rock.
Disconformities occur between parallel sedimentary layers and are often subtle.
quiz.why: A disconformity is between PARALLEL layers. Tilted layers below flat ones is an angular unconformity.

quiz.q: At Siccar Point, Scotland, vertical Ordovician sandstone is overlain by gently dipping Devonian redbeds. What does this contact show?
options: A disconformity with about 5 million years missing
A nonconformity with about 50 million years missing
A conformable contact with no time missing
An angular unconformity with about 50 million years missing
An angular unconformity with about 500 million years missing
quiz.why: Tilted older strata under flatter younger strata is an angular unconformity. The missing time is 50 million years.

quiz.q: Why does tilted sedimentary rock tell us it was deformed AFTER it was deposited?
options: Sediment always settles at an angle in water
Sediment settles flat, so the tilt must have come later (original horizontality)
Superposition says tilted beds are older
Baked contacts tilt beds when they form
quiz.why: Original horizontality: sediment piles up in flat beds. A bed that is tilted now was moved after it formed.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the best index fossil?
options: A species found in one valley that lived 300 million years
A species that never became extinct
A species found worldwide that lived only a few million years
A species that lived for hundreds of millions of years worldwide
A species found in a single bed in one country
quiz.why: A good index fossil is widespread geographically and lived a short time, so its presence marks a narrow age.

quiz.q: A mineral starts with only parent isotope. After 3 half-lives, what fraction of the original parent remains?
quiz.why: Each half-life halves the parent: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8.

quiz.q: A granite contains 25% of its original 40K and 75% 40Ar daughter. Using a half-life of 1.3 billion years for 40K, how old is the mineral?
quiz.why: 25% is 1/4, which is 2 half-lives. 2 x 1.3 billion = 2.6 billion years.

quiz.q: A zircon has 12.5% of its original 235U left. Using a half-life of 713 million years, what is the age?
quiz.why: 12.5% is 1/8, which is 3 half-lives. 3 x 713 million is about 2.14 billion years.

quiz.q: A piece of wood has 1/4 of its original 14C. Using 5,730 years for the half-life, how old is it?
quiz.why: 1/4 is 2 half-lives. 2 x 5,730 = 11,460 years.
quiz.source: Textbook 7.2.1, 7.2.2 (14C value is from the textbook, not the slide table)

quiz.q: Which isotope system in the table of isotopes used for dating has the SHORTEST half-life?
quiz.why: 713 million years is the smallest number in the table.

quiz.q: A mineral is reheated above its closure temperature and then cools again. What does its isotopic date most likely give?
options: The original age of the Earth
The time it last cooled below the closure temperature (the clock was reset)
The age of the oldest rock it formed from
Always the same age as before it was reheated
The age of the nearest fossil
quiz.why: Isotopic dating gives the time a mineral began to keep all its parent and daughter atoms. Reheating can reset it.

quiz.q: Which rock type is BEST for direct radiometric dating?
quiz.why: Igneous and metamorphic rocks are best. Sedimentary rocks are made of grains from older rocks and are rarely dated directly.

quiz.q: A sandstone lies above a lava flow dated 54 Ma and below a volcanic ash dated 50 Ma. What age range does the sandstone have?
options: It cannot be dated at all
quiz.why: Superposition: the sandstone is younger than the lava below it and older than the ash above it. This is bracketing.

quiz.q: A 65 million year old basalt dike cuts across a sedimentary sequence. What does this say about the strata?
options: They are younger than 65 million years
They are exactly 65 million years old
They are older than 65 million years
They are the same age as the dike
Nothing, strata cannot be compared to a dike
quiz.why: Cross-cutting: the dike is younger than what it cuts, so the strata are older than 65 Ma.

quiz.q: Which dating method fits a 7,000 year old charred bone from an archaeological site?
quiz.why: The bone is organic and young. The other isotope systems have half-lives of hundreds of millions to billions of years, too long to be useful for 7,000 years.

quiz.q: Which dating method is best for a 2.5 billion year old zircon in a granite?
quiz.why: Zircon holds uranium, and 238U (4.5 billion years) or 235U (713 million years) have half-lives suited to such an age. 14C is useful only to about 57,000 years.

quiz.q:
Which of these methods give numerical ages WITHOUT radioactive isotopes?
I. Counting tree rings
II. Counting annual varves
III. Potassium to argon dating
quiz.why: Tree rings and varves are counted and have a limited range. K-Ar uses radioactive 40K.

quiz.q: The age of the Earth, 4.57 Ga, was determined from...
options: The oldest rock on Earth's surface at 4.03 Ga
Correlation with meteorites and moon rocks
quiz.why: Earth's oldest rocks are younger than the planet, because of recycling. Meteorites and moon rocks preserve the early solar system age.

quiz.q: Which lists the geologic time units from LARGEST to SMALLEST?
quiz.why: Eons are largest (hundreds to thousands of Ma), then eras, periods, and epochs.

quiz.q: The principle of lateral continuity states that...
options: A sedimentary layer cut by a valley can be assumed to have once spanned the gap
The latissimus dorsi wraps around the whole body
A road will usually continue around the next corner
The Sun will come up in the morning
quiz.why: Strata form wide sheets, and later erosion dissects them. The Kaibab, Coconino and Hermit layers match across the Grand Canyon.

quiz.q: Rock A is beach sandstone and rock B is deep sea mudstone, far apart, and both formed at the same time. Which type of correlation matches them?
options: Biostratigraphic correlation only if both are limestone
None, since the rock types differ
quiz.why: Chronostratigraphic correlation matches rocks of the same age even if their lithology (rock type) differs, because different environments exist at the same time.

quiz.q: After one half-life the daughter-to-parent ratio is 1. What is it after three half-lives?
quiz.why: After 3 half-lives, 12.5% parent and 87.5% daughter. 87.5 / 12.5 = 7.

order.title: Warm-up: four flat layers
order.prompt: A road cut shows four flat, undeformed sedimentary layers. Conglomerate is at the very bottom. Limestone is at the very top. The sandstone lies directly on the shale. Put the layers in the order they were deposited.
order.why: Original horizontality: the beds were laid flat and are undeformed. Superposition: each bed is older than the one above it. The conglomerate is at the bottom so it is oldest, and the limestone is at the top so it is youngest. The sandstone sits on the shale, so the shale is older than the sandstone.

order.title: A dike through layers
order.prompt: Three flat layers: the shale is at the bottom, the sandstone sits on the shale, and the limestone sits on the sandstone. A vertical basalt dike cuts through all three layers. Order the four events.
order.why: Superposition gives shale, then sandstone, then limestone, because each lies on the one before. Cross-cutting relations: the dike cuts all three layers, so it is younger than all of them and goes last.

order.title: Pluton, dike and fault
order.prompt: Sandstone lies below shale in a stack of flat beds. A granite pluton cuts both beds, has a baked contact in both, and holds xenoliths of both. A basalt dike cuts through the granite and both beds. A fault offsets the dike, the granite and the beds. Order the five events.
order.why: Superposition: sandstone is below shale, so sandstone is older. Baked contacts and inclusions (xenoliths): the beds were there first, so the granite is younger than both. Cross-cutting: the dike cuts the granite, so the dike is younger than the granite. The fault offsets the dike and everything else, so it is the youngest event.

order.title: Angular unconformity
order.prompt: A cliff shows tilted sandstone with tilted shale lying on top of it. A flat erosion surface cuts across the edges of the tilted beds. A flat-lying conglomerate rests on that surface and is not tilted. Order the five events.
order.why: Original horizontality: both tilted beds were laid flat, so the tilting came after their deposition, and superposition puts the sandstone before the shale. The flat erosion surface truncates the tilted beds (cross-cutting), so the erosion is younger than the tilting. The conglomerate sits on that surface and is not tilted, so it was deposited last. Together this forms an angular unconformity.

order.title: Basement, nonconformity and dike
order.prompt: Folded gneiss is cut by a granite intrusion that contains xenoliths of the gneiss and has a baked contact in it. An erosion surface truncates both the gneiss and the granite. Sandstone rests on that surface and contains granite pebbles. Shale lies on the sandstone. A basalt dike cuts the gneiss, granite, sandstone and shale. Order the six events.
order.why: Gneiss first. The xenoliths and baked contact show the granite is younger than the gneiss (inclusions, baked contacts). The erosion surface cuts both, so it is younger than both (cross-cutting). The sandstone lies on that surface and holds granite pebbles, so it is younger than the granite and the erosion. Shale lies on the sandstone (superposition). The dike cuts everything, so it is last. The contact of sandstone on crystalline rock is a nonconformity.

order.title: Disconformity, sill and fault
order.prompt: A limestone bed is overlain by parallel mudstone beds. The contact between them is an uneven surface with channels cut into the limestone, and the mudstone contains limestone pebbles. A rhyolite sill sits inside the mudstone with mudstone xenoliths and a baked contact. A fault offsets the sill, the mudstone and the limestone. A basalt dike crosses the fault with no offset. Order the six events.
order.why: The channels cut the limestone, so the erosion is younger than the limestone (cross-cutting). The mudstone fills the channels and holds limestone pebbles, so it is younger than the erosion (inclusions, superposition). Parallel beds with an erosion surface between them make a disconformity. The sill has mudstone xenoliths and a baked contact, so it is younger than the mudstone. The fault offsets the sill, so it is younger than the sill. The dike crosses the fault without being offset, so it is younger than the fault and is last.
